course.title: AP Precalculus
course.description: Build the function toolkit that calculus depends on: how quantities change together, polynomial and rational functions, exponential and logarithmic models, and trigonometric and polar functions.
course.previewDescription: Study how outputs change with inputs, then use polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions to describe patterns and build models.

unit.title: Polynomial and Rational Functions

topic.title: Rational Functions and Zeros
topic.summary: Finding the zeros of a rational function and using signs to decide where it is positive or negative.

lesson.title: Rational Functions and Zeros
lesson.summary: Finding the zeros of a rational function and using signs to decide where it is positive or negative.
learningGoals: Find the zeros of a rational function from its numerator, and exclude inputs where the denominator is zero.
Use a sign chart to decide where a rational function is positive or negative.
Solve rational inequalities and write the solution with the correct endpoints.
lesson.bigIdea: A rational function can change sign only at a zero of the numerator or at an input where the denominator is zero. Finding those inputs splits the number line into intervals where the sign stays the same.
lesson.context: A quotient is zero only when the numerator is zero and the quotient exists. That gives a short checklist for locating zeros, and the same inputs mark the boundaries between positive and negative stretches.

sections.title: A zero of a rational function is a zero of the numerator that is not excluded by the denominator.

blocks.text: A fraction equals 0 only when its numerator equals 0 and the fraction is defined. So the zeros of the rational function r(x) = p(x)/q(x) are the zeros of p(x) at which q(x) is not 0. For r(x) = (x − 2)(x + 3)/(x − 1), the zeros are x = 2 and x = −3. The input x = 1 makes the denominator zero, so r(1) does not exist.

blocks.title: Check the denominator before you call it a zero
blocks.text: For r(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) = (x − 1)(x + 1)/(x − 1), the numerator is zero at both x = 1 and x = −1. But r(1) is undefined, so x = 1 is not a zero. The only zero is x = −1. Topic 1.10 explains what the graph does at x = 1.

sections.takeaway: Set the numerator equal to 0, then throw out any solution that also makes the denominator 0.

sections.title: A sign chart records whether the function is positive or negative on each interval.

blocks.text: Take r(x) = (x + 2)(x − 1)/(x − 4). The numerator is zero at x = −2 and x = 1, and the denominator is zero at x = 4. These three inputs split the number line into four intervals. On each interval, r(x) cannot change sign, so one test value tells you the sign of the whole interval.

The sign does not always change at a zero. A factor with even multiplicity, such as (x − 2)² in r(x) = (x − 2)²(x + 1)/(x − 5), touches the axis at x = 2 without crossing it, so the sign stays the same on both sides. The same idea applies to a repeated factor in the denominator.

sections.takeaway: Mark every zero of the numerator and denominator, test one value in each interval, and watch for even multiplicity.

sections.title: A rational inequality is solved by choosing the intervals with the right sign.

blocks.text: To solve r(x) ≥ 0 for the function above, read the sign chart. The function is positive on −2 < x < 1 and on x > 4. It equals 0 at x = −2 and x = 1, and those inputs satisfy the inequality. It is undefined at x = 4, so that input never belongs to the solution. The solution is [−2, 1] ∪ (4, ∞).

blocks.title: Endpoint rules
items: Include a zero of the numerator when the inequality is ≥ or ≤.
Exclude a zero of the numerator when the inequality is > or <.
Always exclude an input where the denominator is 0.

sections.takeaway: Use the sign chart for the intervals, then decide each endpoint with the endpoint rules.

vocabulary.definition: A table that records whether a function is positive or negative on each interval between its zeros and its undefined inputs.
An input chosen inside an interval to find the sign of a function on the whole interval.

connections.title: Multiplicity decides whether the sign changes
connections.body: In Topic 1.5, an odd-multiplicity zero made a polynomial cross the x-axis and an even-multiplicity zero made it touch. The same rule applies to the factors of a numerator and a denominator.
connections.transferQuestion: At a zero where the factor appears twice, does the sign of the function change?
connections.feedback: No. A factor with even multiplicity touches the axis and the function keeps the same sign on both sides.

connections.title: The undefined inputs come next
connections.body: In this topic you excluded inputs where the denominator is zero. Topic 1.9 studies what the graph does near them, and a sign chart helps again.
connections.transferQuestion: Why might the graph shoot upward on one side of an undefined input and downward on the other?
connections.feedback: The sign of the function can differ on the two sides, while the size of the outputs is very large near the input.

glossary.definition: An input whose output is 0. A real zero is also an x-intercept of the graph.
A function that can be written as a quotient of two polynomials, with a denominator that is not the zero polynomial.
A table that records whether a function is positive or negative on each interval between its zeros and its undefined inputs.
An input chosen inside an interval to find the sign of a function on the whole interval.
